paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns from an existing dataset, making errors in that dataset a direct obstacle to learning useful behavior. ADG addresses corruption that can affect high-dimensional states or several parts of the data simultaneously. Its starting point is that diffusion models can remove noise, but training them directly on corrupted examples can make them fit the corruption instead.

The method separates recovery into three stages. First, an ambient diffusion model learns from partially corrupted data using approximated distributions, with theoretical guarantees. Its noise predictions then help distinguish clean examples from corrupted ones. The identified clean subset trains a standard diffusion model, which subsequently refines the examples marked as corrupted.

This makes ADG a dataset-recovery procedure that the authors describe as compatible with any offline reinforcement learning algorithm. Experiments on MuJoCo, Kitchen, and Adroit report stronger robustness across different noise settings and state-of-the-art results. The findings support improving the training data itself as a way to reduce the downstream effects of corruption.
neurips-2025-adg-ambient-diffusion-guide.tldr: ADG uses a staged diffusion process to identify and repair corrupted offline reinforcement learning data, improving robustness in benchmark experiments.

paragraphs: An agent choosing an external tool relies on information such as its name, description, and parameter schema. This paper shows that those descriptions can themselves become an attack surface: an adversary can make a malicious tool unusually appealing without accessing the model's internals or using prompt injection.

The proposed Attractive Metadata Attack iteratively generates and improves tool metadata through a black-box, in-context learning framework. The resulting metadata remains syntactically and semantically valid and fits into ordinary tool ecosystems without changes to the agent's execution framework. This matters because the attack influences a normal selection step rather than requiring a visibly broken interface.

Across ten realistic simulated scenarios and several popular agents, the authors report attack success rates of 81–95%, significant privacy leakage, and negligible disruption to the primary task. The attack also remains effective against the evaluated prompt defenses, auditors, and structured selection protocols. These results motivate defenses at execution time: successful task completion and apparently valid tool descriptions do not, in these experiments, prevent malicious tool selection.
neurips-2025-attractive-metadata-attack-.tldr: Manipulating otherwise valid tool metadata can steer LLM agents toward malicious tools while leaving their main tasks largely unaffected.

paragraphs: Unsupervised person re-identification learns to match images of people without identity labels. Memory-bank methods support this learning by maintaining representations initialized from clusters. Existing updates move these stored representations toward positive examples, encouraging members of a cluster to stay close together. The paper argues that this leaves a second requirement insufficiently addressed: different clusters also need distinct representations.

BMW updates the memory bank using two explicit objectives. One reduces variation within a class; the other increases separation between classes. The authors formulate these updates as gradient descent and design the separation objective to work effectively even when only a limited number of rewriting steps are available, particularly a single update.

The intended benefit is a better set of stored reference representations for training discriminative image features. Experiments on standard benchmarks support the approach's effectiveness in unsupervised re-identification, including results exceeding previous methods with stronger backbones. The contribution therefore concerns how the training memory is maintained, showing that its update rule can materially affect the features learned from it.
neurips-2025-bmw-bidirectionally-memory-.tldr: BMW improves unsupervised person re-identification by updating memory banks to make each class more compact and different classes more distinct.

paragraphs: Sparse rewards make reinforcement learning difficult because useful feedback may arrive too infrequently to guide behavior efficiently. Reward shaping addresses this by adding informative intermediate rewards. This paper uses that idea to connect learning across multiple tasks, with a centralized reward agent supporting several distributed policy agents.

The centralized agent acts as a shared store of knowledge distilled from different tasks. It communicates that knowledge through shaped reward signals, which give individual policy agents additional feedback during learning. The key design choice is the form of what gets shared: rewards encode useful knowledge in a signal that each policy agent can use while learning its own task.

The framework also transfers meaningful reward signals to new tasks. Evaluations cover discrete and continuous domains, including Meta-World, and demonstrate robustness in the tested multi-task settings with sparse rewards and effective transfer to unseen tasks. These findings support reward generation as a practical mechanism for both sharing existing task knowledge and helping agents learn beyond the original set of tasks.
neurips-2025-centralized-reward-agent-fo.tldr: A centralized reward agent shares knowledge through informative reward signals, improving multi-task learning and transfer in sparse-reward experiments.

paragraphs: Language models often train on broad web data mixed with a smaller amount of knowledge-dense material. This paper asks whether learning from that smaller source improves smoothly as model size or its share of training data increases. Controlled experiments mixing synthetic biographies with web data show that knowledge acquisition can instead change abruptly.

At a critical model size, the tested models shift from memorizing very few biographies to memorizing most of them. A similar threshold appears in the mixing ratio: below it, extensive training yields little memorization; above it, acquisition increases rapidly. These observations concern the mixed-data setting and differ from the behavior described for training exclusively on knowledge-dense data.

The authors explain the transitions through limited capacity being allocated across competing datasets. Their information-theoretic framework predicts discontinuous allocation changes and a power-law relationship between the critical mixing ratio and model size. The practical implication is specific but consequential: a mixture that works well for a large model may be poorly suited to a smaller one, and the reverse can also occur.
neurips-2025-data-mixing-can-induce-phas.tldr: Controlled experiments show that learning knowledge from mixed datasets can change abruptly at thresholds in model size and data proportions.

paragraphs: Optimal transport provides both distances between probability distributions and plans describing how to move one distribution toward another. Computing those plans can be expensive. Slicing methods simplify the problem through lower-dimensional views. A method called min-SWGG builds a multidimensional plan from a single one-dimensional plan, then chooses the slice giving the smallest Wasserstein distance.

The paper addresses two obstacles in this approach: the number of slices needed grows exponentially with dimension, and the projections are restricted to linear ones. The authors recast slice selection as a bilevel optimization problem, with one optimization nested inside another. They introduce a differentiable approximation that enables efficient search for the optimal slice, including in high-dimensional settings.

A generalized extension also accommodates data on manifolds, where the relevant geometry need not fit a simple linear projection. Applications include gradient flows on manifolds and in high-dimensional spaces, plus image generation through sliced transport-based conditional flow matching. These demonstrations show why efficient approximate transport plans matter beyond measuring distances: the plans can become working components of learning and generation procedures.
neurips-2025-differentiable-generalized-.tldr: A differentiable optimization approach makes sliced transport-plan estimation more practical in high dimensions and extends it to manifold-valued data.

paragraphs: A medical imaging model may encounter images unlike those used in training, making its predictions unreliable. Comparing a new image directly with training data could help detect this mismatch. In practice, the training database often cannot accompany the deployed model because of its size, ownership restrictions, or privacy constraints.

The Isolation Network turns this comparison into a binary classification problem: it measures how difficult it is to separate a particular test image from training examples. DIsoN distributes that procedure between the training and deployment locations, exchanging model parameters while keeping the data at their respective sites. A further variant restricts comparison to training examples from the test image's predicted class.

The authors evaluate the method on twelve detection tasks across dermatology, chest X-ray, breast ultrasound, and histopathology datasets. They report favorable performance against existing methods while respecting data privacy. The broader proposal is an accompanying service for deployed models: developers could make their retained training data useful for remote detection of unfamiliar inputs without shipping the database itself.
neurips-2025-dison-decentralized-isolati.tldr: DIsoN detects unfamiliar medical images by comparing them with remotely held training data through model-parameter exchanges.

paragraphs: Error-feedback algorithms are widely used in efficient neural-network training, but their theoretical analyses often assume a form of smoothness that does not capture the objectives encountered in those problems. This paper studies normalized error feedback under generalized smoothness, aiming to bring convergence theory closer to the settings where these algorithms are actually used.

The authors propose distributed algorithms that use normalization and establish an O(1/√K) convergence rate for nonconvex problems. Their analysis does not require conditions on data heterogeneity across participating nodes. It also allows stepsize tuning without knowledge of problem parameters, and provides convergence guarantees when the training process involves stochastic gradients.

The theoretical results are paired with experiments on polynomial minimization, logistic regression, and ResNet-20 training. The normalized algorithms outperform their non-normalized counterparts in these tasks, which the authors connect to the larger stepsizes their methods permit. The contribution combines a broader mathematical justification with evidence that normalization can improve practical optimization, rather than serving solely as a technical device in the analysis.
neurips-2025-error-feedback-under-l-0-l-.tldr: Normalized distributed error-feedback algorithms gain convergence guarantees under generalized smoothness and outperform non-normalized versions in the reported tasks.

paragraphs: Detecting misleading videos requires interpreting both visual material and associated text. The paper identifies two obstacles: a shortage of large, diverse datasets and methods that rely too heavily on fixed templates instead of reasoning about deceptive content. It addresses both with a new benchmark and a dedicated training framework.

The benchmark, FakeVV, contains more than 100,000 video-text pairs with detailed annotations intended to support interpretable analysis. The proposed model framework, Fact-R1, follows three training stages. It first learns from misinformation instructions containing extended reasoning, then undergoes Direct Preference Optimization, and finally uses Group Relative Policy Optimization with a newly designed verifiable reward function.

This sequence connects examples of reasoning, preference alignment, and reinforcement learning guided by checkable rewards. The authors report emergent reasoning behaviors comparable to those seen in advanced text-based reinforcement learning systems, now in a multimodal misinformation setting. The stated contribution is a combined basis for studying detection and explanation: richer video-text evidence, reasoning-oriented training, and verification are developed together.
neurips-2025-fact-r1-towards-explainable.tldr: Fact-R1 combines a large annotated video-text benchmark with staged reasoning and reinforcement learning for explainable misinformation detection.

paragraphs: Data valuation asks how much particular training data contributes to a machine learning model. Data Shapley addresses this at the level of individual examples, but providers often contribute batches. The paper studies the resulting group-valuation problem and identifies a vulnerability in existing extensions: a provider can split a contribution into multiple groups to unfairly increase its valuation.

The authors call this a shell company attack because the apparent number of contributors can change without a corresponding change in the underlying contribution. They introduce Faithful Group Shapley Value, or FGSV, and establish its unique defense against this form of manipulation. The central concern is whether a valuation remains faithful when a provider strategically reorganizes its data.

To make the proposed value computationally usable, the paper also develops an approximation algorithm with guarantees of speed and accuracy. Experiments report substantially better computational efficiency and approximation accuracy than state-of-the-art methods. The combined result addresses both parts of the problem: a group valuation resistant to strategic splitting and a practical way to estimate it.
neurips-2025-faithful-group-shapley-valu.tldr: Faithful Group Shapley Value resists inflated valuations from strategic group splitting and comes with a fast, accurate approximation algorithm.

paragraphs: Many decision problems first predict unknown quantities and then optimize using those predictions. Decision-focused learning trains the predictor according to the quality of the resulting decisions. When the predicted quantities appear in constraints, prediction errors can also make the chosen decision infeasible. This paper develops a framework that explicitly balances those two concerns.

The framework applies to generic constrained optimization problems without assuming they are linear or integer linear programs. It introduces two losses derived from maximum likelihood estimation. One penalizes predictions that produce infeasible solutions. The other penalizes predictions that exclude the true optimal solution, addressing a different failure: an inaccurate feasible region can rule out the best decision.

A single adjustable parameter combines the losses and lets a decision-maker emphasize feasibility or decision quality. Experiments across several constrained optimization instances demonstrate control over this trade-off. With suitable choices of the parameter, the method exceeds existing baselines on the prioritized objective. The result is a tunable approach to competing goals, rather than a claim that one setting simultaneously optimizes both.
neurips-2025-feasibility-aware-decision-.tldr: Two complementary training losses let prediction-driven optimization balance feasible decisions against decision quality.

paragraphs: Most detectors frame human and machine writing as two classes to distinguish. This paper argues that the human class is too diverse to represent adequately with a limited training sample. A detector may consequently learn quirks of the sampled human texts and generalize poorly to different writers, domains, or generating models.

The authors instead treat machine-generated text as the reference distribution and human writing as out-of-distribution input. Their framework explores one-class learning methods, including DeepSVDD and HRN, alongside energy-based scoring. The conceptual shift is to characterize machine writing and detect departures from it, rather than assume that sampled human writing captures a coherent opposing class.

On the DeepFake dataset, the approach reports 98.3% for both AUROC and AUPR, with 8.9% FPR95. Additional experiments cover multilingual text, attacked inputs, unseen generating models, and unseen domains, supporting robustness and generalization in those settings. The title's description of human texts as outliers is therefore a detection formulation relative to the learned machine-text distribution, not a claim about the intrinsic quality of human writing.
neurips-2025-human-texts-are-outliers-de.tldr: Treating human writing as outside a learned machine-text distribution improves detection generalization in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Facility location mechanisms choose where to place a facility for a group of agents. This paper studies choices guided by predictions of the optimal solution, focusing on fairness through the envy ratio: the largest ratio between any two agents' utilities. That objective directs attention to disparities between people rather than only aggregate or worst-case utility.

For deterministic mechanisms, the authors give a parameterized trade-off between consistency and robustness. Consistency describes the guarantee when the prediction is correct; robustness describes protection when it is unreliable. Their mechanism achieves α-consistency and α/(α−1)-robustness for α in [1,2], and they prove its optimality. The expression exposes how stronger reliance on predictions affects the worst-case guarantee.

The paper also develops a randomized mechanism without predictions, improving the best-known approximation ratio from 2 to 1.8944 and resolving previously open questions. Building on that result, it introduces a randomized mechanism that uses predictions for improved guarantees. Together, these results characterize ways to combine predictive information, randomization, and a fairness objective in facility placement.
neurips-2025-learning-augmented-facility.tldr: The paper establishes prediction-sensitive fairness guarantees for facility location and improves approximation through randomization.

paragraphs: LiteReality converts indoor scans containing color and depth into compact 3D scenes that can be edited and interacted with. Its goal includes properties needed by graphics workflows: separate objects, articulation, and physically based materials. Those requirements make scene organization and object construction central to the reconstruction process.

The pipeline first interprets the scan and organizes its layout and objects through a structured scene graph. It then retrieves visually similar artist-created models from a curated database. A Material Painting module recovers spatially varying appearances for those assets, after which a simulation engine adds basic physical properties to support interaction.

The authors report state-of-the-art similarity performance on Scan2CAD for their object retrieval module, which requires no training. They also demonstrate appearance transfer under severe misalignment, occlusion, and poor lighting, alongside complete reconstructions from real scans and public datasets. The approach matters because its outputs already have the object structure, materials, and compatibility needed for graphics pipelines, supporting applications such as virtual environments, robotics, and digital twins.
neurips-2025-litereality-graphics-ready-.tldr: LiteReality turns indoor color-and-depth scans into editable, interactive 3D scenes using retrieved assets and recovered materials.

paragraphs: Multi-modality re-identification matches objects using complementary visual sources, but models trained with every source available can lose accuracy when some inputs are missing. Miss-ReID addresses missing modalities during both training and inference. Its central idea is to use a vision-language model to provide semantic representations that compensate for unavailable visual information.

The framework extracts features from the available modalities and maintains identity-specific prototypes in memory banks. It then uses interactions with local image patches to distill object structure that is shared across modalities. That structure is converted into pseudo-word tokens and combined with learned modality prompts to produce personalized textual descriptions.

The vision-language model aligns those descriptions with visual information, while memory-based constraints guide the resulting representations. These text features serve as substitutes at the semantic level for missing visual modalities. Experiments across several missing-modality scenarios show stronger performance than state-of-the-art methods. The contribution is a flexible retrieval framework whose compensation mechanism draws on available object structure and cross-modal alignment, supporting operation when complete visual inputs cannot be assumed.
neurips-2025-miss-reid-delivering-robust.tldr: Miss-ReID uses vision-language alignment to compensate for missing visual modalities during object re-identification training and inference.

paragraphs: Two accounts of algorithmic decision-making point in different directions. Monoculture suggests that models behave so similarly that the same people face exclusion everywhere. Model multiplicity emphasizes that similarly accurate models can make different decisions about individuals. This paper tests how much support each account receives when language models perform prediction tasks.

The study evaluates fifty language models, including open models ranging from one billion to 141 billion parameters and leading commercial systems. It uses four prompt variations across six prediction tasks and examines both existing and new quantitative measures of similarity and variation. This setup considers differences between models as well as differences produced by prompting a single model.

The results fall between the two extremes. Model similarity is observable, but systematic exclusion without recourse is rare in the evaluated setting. Prompt changes also introduce some prediction diversity even when the underlying model remains fixed. The findings give empirical support to parts of both narratives while suggesting that neither complete uniformity nor unrestricted variation adequately describes the studied ecosystem.
neurips-2025-monoculture-or-multiplicity.tldr: An evaluation of fifty language models finds meaningful prediction similarity alongside diversity, supporting neither strict monoculture nor dominant multiplicity.

paragraphs: Transformer inference retains keys and values from earlier sequence positions in a cache. That cache grows with sequence length and can become a memory bottleneck. Multi-head latent attention compresses the stored representations into a smaller latent space; this paper adds compression across time, reducing the number of temporal representations that must remain in memory.

Multi-head Temporal Latent Attention uses a hyper-network to dynamically merge cache vectors from adjacent positions. Merging creates a mismatch between the compressed cache and the original sequence length. A stride-aware causal mask handles that mismatch, allowing parallel training while maintaining consistency with how the model operates during inference.

Experiments span speech translation, recognition, understanding, and text summarization. MTLA achieves competitive performance against standard multi-head attention while improving inference speed and GPU memory use. In the reported English-to-German speech translation example, it delivers a 5.3-fold speedup and reduces memory use by a factor of 8.3 while maintaining translation quality. These results show the practical value of compressing both representation size and temporal storage.
neurips-2025-multi-head-temporal-latent-.tldr: MTLA merges neighboring attention-cache entries to reduce memory and accelerate inference while preserving competitive task performance.

paragraphs: Training a model to produce intermediate reasoning requires sampling possible reasoning paths. Existing reward-ranked fine-tuning methods often spend the same sampling budget on every prompt, despite differences in difficulty and learning progress. This paper identifies that static allocation as a source of inefficient, noisy gradient estimates.

GVM-RAFT allocates samples separately for each prompt under a fixed computational budget. It monitors acceptance rates and stochastic gradient norms, using those signals to minimize gradient variance. The aim is to make each unit of sampling computation contribute more effectively to the training update, rather than distribute effort uniformly across prompts.

The theoretical analysis establishes faster convergence guarantees under suitable conditions. In mathematical reasoning experiments, GVM-RAFT achieves a two- to four-fold speedup and considerable accuracy improvements over vanilla RAFT. The same allocation strategy can also be incorporated into other reinforcement learning algorithms, with GRPO showing similar improvements in convergence and test accuracy. The findings connect training efficiency to how computation is distributed across examples, alongside the choice of learning algorithm.
neurips-2025-optimizing-chain-of-thought.tldr: GVM-RAFT improves reasoning training by allocating prompt-specific sampling budgets to reduce gradient variance.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation assigns classes to image pixels, but evaluation usually measures overlap between whole predicted and reference masks. Choosing each pixel's most likely class does not directly optimize those overlap metrics. RankSEG addresses this mismatch through procedures targeting Dice and intersection over union, but its computational cost limits practical use.

This paper introduces a reciprocal moment approximation, producing RankSEG-RMA. It reduces the complexity of both metric-specific procedures to O(d), where d is the number of pixels, while retaining comparable performance. That replaces RankDice's O(d log d) computation with a substantial constant factor and RankIoU's O(d²) computation.

The authors also address RankSEG's restriction to overlapping segmentation, where a pixel may belong to several classes. A pixel-wise score inspired by the approximation enables efficient use when classes must be mutually exclusive, as in standard benchmarks. Evaluations across datasets and modern models demonstrate effectiveness. Together, the changes make metric-aware segmentation more computationally accessible and extend it to a common form of the task.
neurips-2025-rankseg-rma-an-efficient-se.tldr: RankSEG-RMA makes overlap-metric-aware segmentation linear in pixel count and extends it to mutually exclusive pixel classes.

paragraphs: This paper studies the computational difficulty of finding stationary points and equilibria in settings where teams have opposing objectives. It focuses especially on symmetry: whether a symmetric problem admits equilibria that algorithms can find while preserving that symmetry. Its results classify the difficulty of several closely related equilibrium problems.

For a team of two players facing one adversary, computing an approximate Nash equilibrium is CLS-complete. The proof uses the adversary to enforce symmetry in a reduction from a two-player identical-payoff game, while preserving the required game structure. The constructed instances are polymatrix games, so the classification also applies within that restricted class.

For symmetric min-max problems, computing symmetric first-order equilibria is PPAD-complete even with quadratic functions. Related hardness holds for symmetric approximate equilibria in six-player, three-versus-three games. The authors derive a barrier to convergence for symmetric dynamics, encompassing many studied algorithms. Finally, finding a non-symmetric inverse-polynomial-accuracy equilibrium in symmetric min-max optimization is FNP-hard. Together, the results show that symmetry does not by itself make equilibrium computation tractable.
neurips-2025-the-complexity-of-symmetric.tldr: The paper establishes computational hardness classifications for symmetric and non-symmetric equilibria in min-max optimization and opposing-team games.

paragraphs: Adding layers to a language model does not necessarily make its deeper layers contribute as much as expected. This paper examines that phenomenon across Llama, Mistral, DeepSeek, and Qwen families. Its theoretical and empirical analysis identifies Pre-Layer Normalization, a widely used technique for stabilizing training, as the underlying cause.

The authors trace the problem to output variance that grows exponentially with depth. In their analysis, this causes the derivatives of deep Transformer blocks to become identity matrices, so those blocks contribute little to training. They propose LayerNorm Scaling, which scales the normalization output variance inversely with the square root of layer depth to mitigate that growth.

Experiments on models from 130 million to seven billion parameters show significantly better pretraining performance than Pre-Layer Normalization, with improvements carrying into supervised fine-tuning. The authors attribute the gains to deeper layers participating more effectively in training. The practical insight is that the usefulness of model depth depends partly on normalization behavior, and a simple depth-dependent adjustment can improve it in the evaluated models.
neurips-2025-the-curse-of-depth-in-large.tldr: LayerNorm Scaling addresses depth-related variance growth so deeper language-model layers contribute more effectively during training.

paragraphs: Time-series foundation models must forecast sequences whose behavior may change across domains or over time. The paper argues that existing models lack effective adaptation mechanisms for these shifts. TS-RAG adds retrieval so a forecasting model can draw on relevant examples without requiring task-specific fine-tuning.

The framework uses pretrained time-series encoders to find semantically relevant segments in a dedicated knowledge base. These segments enrich the context available for the current input. An Adaptive Retrieval Mixer then dynamically combines the retrieved patterns with the foundation model's internal representation, connecting external examples to the model's existing forecasting capabilities.

Across seven public benchmark datasets, the authors report state-of-the-art zero-shot forecasting performance and improvements of up to 6.84% over existing time-series foundation models. They also report useful interpretability from the retrieval-based framework. The findings support retrieval as a way to improve generalization across the evaluated domains while making the contextual patterns informing a forecast more accessible, without adapting the model separately to each target task.
neurips-2025-ts-rag-retrieval-augmented-.tldr: TS-RAG retrieves relevant time-series patterns and adaptively mixes them into foundation-model representations to improve zero-shot forecasts.

paragraphs: UltraVideo targets video generation through improvements to the training material itself. The dataset combines high-resolution imagery with detailed text descriptions, addressing the paper's premise that image quality, resolution, and caption detail strongly influence generated videos. It contains UHD-4K video, with 22.4% of the collection at 8K, and covers more than one hundred topic categories.

Each video receives nine structured captions and a summary caption, with an average caption length reported as 824 words. The authors build the collection through four largely automated stages: gathering diverse high-quality clips, filtering using statistics, purifying with models, and producing comprehensive structured captions. This connects visual curation with detailed descriptions of the resulting material.

The paper also extends Wan into UltraWan-1K and UltraWan-4K, which natively generate videos at the corresponding resolutions. The authors report high-quality outputs and more consistent control through text, using these models to demonstrate the effectiveness of the data curation. The contribution therefore pairs a publicly available dataset with generation models that show how the curated material can support UHD video synthesis.
neurips-2025-ultravideo-high-quality-uhd.tldr: UltraVideo pairs curated UHD footage with detailed captions and supports UltraWan models for native 1K and 4K video generation.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can recognize features yet associate them with the wrong objects or positions. This binding problem affects counting, search, descriptions, and spatial reasoning. The paper links it partly to processing visual features in parallel without sufficient mechanisms for sequential attention grounded in image locations.

VISER changes the input by adding low-level spatial structure and pairing it with a prompt encouraging sequential, spatially aware inspection. It uses a single inference query. The key idea is that reasoning can improve when the image itself provides organizational support, alongside verbal instructions about how to examine it.

For GPT-4o, the reported improvements are 25.0% in visual search, 26.8% in counting, and 9.5% in spatial relationships, with scene-description edit-distance error reduced by 0.32 on 2D datasets. Experiments identify the visual modification as essential to these gains; text-only strategies, including chain-of-thought prompting, are insufficient and can worsen results. The findings support visual input design as an effective route to better compositional and spatial reasoning in the tested settings.
neurips-2025-visual-structures-help-visu.tldr: VISER improves visual reasoning by adding spatial structure to images and prompting models to inspect them sequentially.

paragraphs: High-quality faces produced by diffusion models create a forensic challenge that extends beyond deciding whether an image is fake. VLForgery organizes analysis around three questions: whether a face was falsified, which regions were synthesized, and which generator produced the synthesis. It uses multimodal language models to connect visual evidence with structured analysis.

The authors introduce VLF, a diverse synthetic-face dataset designed for interaction between visual and language modalities. Their EkCot description method incorporates knowledge from the image-generation pipeline to help models interpret image content. A separate low-level comparison pipeline identifies differences between real and generated images that the multimodal models can use.

Those differential features are incorporated into EkCot to support an ordered process of detection, localization, and attribution. Experiments show higher detection accuracy than other state-of-the-art forensic approaches, while indicating additional potential for localizing falsified regions and analyzing their origin. The strength of the reported evidence therefore differs across the three goals: detection has demonstrated comparative gains, while the broader forensic capabilities are presented as promising extensions.
neurips-2025-vlforgery-face-triad-detect.tldr: VLForgery combines generation knowledge and visual comparisons to improve fake-face detection and support localization and generator attribution.
